Tutorial

Frequency domain decomposition

Frequency domain decomposition (FDD) estimates vibration modes from measured responses. It does not require measurements of the input forces. This guide explains the procedure, its assumptions, and the mathematics behind it.

FDD at a glance

FDD uses vibration records from two or more synchronized sensor channels. It estimates a spectral matrix for the measured responses. It then decomposes this matrix at each frequency.

What you can estimate

  • Frequency: a peak in the first singular value can indicate a resonance.
  • Mode shape: the leading singular vector near an isolated peak estimates the relative motion at the sensors.
  • Damping: enhanced FDD (EFDD) estimates damping from the decay of a selected spectral bell.

The measured shape has an arbitrary scale and phase. An FDD peak is an estimate, and it is not always equal to the natural frequency. See Section 7.3.

How to use this guide

For the procedure, go to FDD, step by step. For measurement and interpretation checks, go to Section 9. For the derivation, start with the assumptions and continue through Sections 1 to 8.

Check each result. A peak can come from a harmonic force or from more than one mode. Noise, sensor placement, and spectral settings also affect the estimate. Use the checks in Section 9 before you report a mode.

The table shows the main steps in the derivation. The assumptions are listed in the next section.

The equation of motion defines the structural model. Its poles describe the modes. The transfer matrix connects the input forces to the measured responses. The response spectral matrix describes those responses in the frequency domain. Near an isolated mode, its leading eigenvector estimates the measured mode shape. Assumptions

The derivation uses the assumptions below. A7 concerns the spectral estimate. A9 and A10 define the approximations for FDD and EFDD. The relevant sections identify where each assumption is used. See also the checks in Section 9.

Model

A0
Output-only. The sensors measure only y(t)y(t)y(t). The input x(t)x(t)x(t) is unknown and has a random model.
A1
Linear, time-invariant, finite-dimensional. The model has nnn coordinates, rrr inputs, and ppp sensors. Displacements from equilibrium are small. The matrices M,C,KM,C,KM,C,K are constant.
A2
Viscous damping. The matrix CCC is constant and symmetric. General damping makes the modes complex. The residue derivation still applies.
A3
Linear input and output maps. Forces enter as BxBxBx. Sensors measure LqLqLq. The model excludes sensor dynamics, delays, and nonlinearities.
A4
Matrix properties. M=MT≻0M=M^T\succ0M=MT≻0, K=KT⪰0K=K^T\succeq0K=KT⪰0, C=CT⪰0C=C^T\succeq0C=CT⪰0; K≻0K\succ0K≻0 if restrained. Derived from energy in §2.4.
A5
Simple, stable eigenvalues. The 2n2n2n eigenvalues are distinct and stable. They occur in conjugate pairs. Each pole is simple. Repeated or defective roots are excluded.

Excitation and measurement

A6
Stationary random excitation. The input xxx has zero mean and is wide-sense stationary. It has finite variance and a spectral density matrix. Ergodicity lets time averages estimate ensemble averages.
A7
Accurate estimate. G^y\widehat G_yGy​ is close to GyG_yGy​; finite-record errors are treated in Appendix D.
A8
Clean, synchronized measurements. Noise is zero or uncorrelated with the response. The channels are synchronized and calibrated.
A9
One dominant mode in the band. Gx(f)≈QxG_x(f)\approx Q_xGx​(f)≈Qx​, and the residual EmE_mEm​ is small relative to the selected term. Made precise in §6.
A10
One mode in the bell. The EFDD bell contains one mode and its correlation decays as a single exponential.

Conventions

A11
Fourier and spectral conventions. j2=−1j^2=-1j2=−1; Fourier transform e−j2πfte^{-j2\pi ft}e−j2πft; GyG_yGy​ two-sided unless marked +^++; one-sided spectra double interior bins but not DC or Nyquist; fff in hertz, ω=2πf\omega=2\pi fω=2πf; displacement PSD in unit2/Hz\text{unit}^2/\text{Hz}unit2/Hz.
A12
Scale and phase are not identified. The shape is known only up to a complex scale. The modal mass cannot be identified.

Part IThe model

1The measurement problem

Sensors record the response y(t)y(t)y(t). The forces x(t)x(t)x(t) are unknown. The aim is to estimate the vibration frequencies, the mode shapes, and the decay rates. A mode shape describes the relative amplitude and phase at the sensors. A single mode has a fixed spatial pattern. When several modes contribute, the pattern can vary with frequency.

FDD estimates the cross-spectral matrix Gy(f)G_y(f)Gy​(f) and decomposes it at each frequency. Near a peak, the dominant direction can estimate a mode shape. EFDD selects a band around a peak and transforms it into a correlation function. The decay of that function gives a damping estimate. The shape is known only up to a complex scale. See §6.

2Energy and the equation of motion

This section derives the equation of motion from energy. It also uses Lagrange’s equations to check the result. The energy model gives the matrix properties used later.

2.1Energy of a vibrating structure

Let q(t)∈Rnq(t)\in\mathbb R^nq(t)∈Rn contain the displacements from static equilibrium. For the linear model, the energy terms are:

T=12q˙TMq˙,V=12qTKq,D=12q˙TCq˙.T=\tfrac12\dot q^TM\dot q,\qquad V=\tfrac12q^TKq,\qquad D=\tfrac12\dot q^TC\dot q.T=21​q˙​TMq˙​,V=21​qTKq,D=21​q˙​TCq˙​.
(2.1)

The matrices MMM, KKK, and CCC represent mass, stiffness, and viscous damping. The external forces do virtual work:

δW=(Bx)Tδq=xTBTδq,\delta W=(Bx)^T\delta q=x^TB^T\delta q,δW=(Bx)Tδq=xTBTδq,

The input matrix BBB has size n×rn\times rn×r. The product BxBxBx is the generalized force. The sensor model is:

y=Lq,y=Lq,y=Lq,

The output matrix LLL has size p×np\times np×n. A Taylor expansion about equilibrium gives the quadratic forms. At a stationary point, the linear term is zero. We can set the constant term to zero. For small displacements, the quadratic term dominates (A1). The energy matrices contain second derivatives and are symmetric.

2.2One degree of freedom

Consider a mass μ>0\mu>0μ>0, spring k>0k>0k>0, and damper b≥0b\ge0b≥0. Let F(t)F(t)F(t) be the force and u(t)u(t)u(t) the displacement. The energy terms and virtual work are:

T=12μu˙2,V=12ku2,D=12bu˙2,δW=F δu.T=\tfrac12\mu\dot u^2,\qquad V=\tfrac12ku^2,\qquad D=\tfrac12b\dot u^2,\qquad \delta W=F\,\delta u.T=21​μu˙2,V=21​ku2,D=21​bu˙2,δW=Fδu.
(2.2)

The rate of stored energy equals the supplied power minus the dissipated power:

ddt(T+V)=Fu˙−bu˙2.\frac{d}{dt}(T+V)=F\dot u-b\dot u^2.dtd​(T+V)=Fu˙−bu˙2.
(2.3)

Differentiate the energy terms and factor the result:

μu˙u¨+kuu˙=Fu˙−bu˙2⟹u˙(μu¨+bu˙+ku−F)=0.\mu\dot u\ddot u+ku\dot u=F\dot u-b\dot u^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\dot u\bigl(\mu\ddot u+b\dot u+ku-F\bigr)=0.μu˙u¨+kuu˙=Fu˙−bu˙2⟹u˙(μu¨+bu˙+ku−F)=0.

When u˙≠0\dot u\ne0u˙=0, divide by u˙\dot uu˙. At an isolated zero of u˙\dot uu˙, continuity of u¨\ddot uu¨ and FFF gives the same result by a limit:

μu¨+bu˙+ku=F.\mu\ddot u+b\dot u+ku=F.μu¨+bu˙+ku=F.
(2.4)

Each term is a force. Divide by μ\muμ to get the normalized equation:

u¨+bμu˙+kμu=Fμ.\ddot u+\frac{b}{\mu}\dot u+\frac{k}{\mu}u=\frac{F}{\mu}.u¨+μb​u˙+μk​u=μF​.

Lagrange’s equations also give this result. They extend to a matrix model. Use the Lagrangian T−VT-VT−V, the dissipation function DDD, and the generalized force QQQ:

ddt∂(T−V)∂u˙−∂(T−V)∂u+∂D∂u˙=Q.\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial (T-V)}{\partial\dot u}-\frac{\partial (T-V)}{\partial u}+\frac{\partial D}{\partial\dot u}=Q.dtd​∂u˙∂(T−V)​−∂u∂(T−V)​+∂u˙∂D​=Q.
(2.5)

For this oscillator, T−V=12μu˙2−12ku2T-V=\tfrac12\mu\dot u^2-\tfrac12ku^2T−V=21​μu˙2−21​ku2, D=12bu˙2D=\tfrac12b\dot u^2D=21​bu˙2, and Q=FQ=FQ=F. The derivatives are:

∂(T−V)∂u˙=μu˙,ddt∂(T−V)∂u˙=μu¨,∂(T−V)∂u=−ku,∂D∂u˙=bu˙.\frac{\partial (T-V)}{\partial\dot u}=\mu\dot u,\qquad \frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial (T-V)}{\partial\dot u}=\mu\ddot u,\qquad \frac{\partial (T-V)}{\partial u}=-ku,\qquad \frac{\partial D}{\partial\dot u}=b\dot u.∂u˙∂(T−V)​=μu˙,dtd​∂u˙∂(T−V)​=μu¨,∂u∂(T−V)​=−ku,∂u˙∂D​=bu˙.

Substitute these derivatives to get (2.4).

2.3Many degrees of freedom

For the full structure, the energy balance is:

ddt(12q˙TMq˙+12qTKq)=q˙TBx−q˙TCq˙.\frac{d}{dt}\left(\tfrac12\dot q^TM\dot q+\tfrac12q^TKq\right)=\dot q^TBx-\dot q^TC\dot q.dtd​(21​q˙​TMq˙​+21​qTKq)=q˙​TBx−q˙​TCq˙​.
(2.6)

The matrices MMM and KKK are constant and symmetric. Thus:

ddt(12q˙TMq˙)=q˙TMq¨,ddt(12qTKq)=q˙TKq.\frac{d}{dt}\left(\tfrac12\dot q^TM\dot q\right)=\dot q^TM\ddot q,\qquad \frac{d}{dt}\left(\tfrac12q^TKq\right)=\dot q^TKq.dtd​(21​q˙​TMq˙​)=q˙​TMq¨​,dtd​(21​qTKq)=q˙​TKq.

Collect the terms:

q˙T(Mq¨+Cq˙+Kq−Bx)=0.\dot q^T\bigl(M\ddot q+C\dot q+Kq-Bx\bigr)=0.q˙​T(Mq¨​+Cq˙​+Kq−Bx)=0.

This equation expresses zero net power along a motion. The energy balance alone does not determine all components of the force equation from one velocity. Lagrange’s equations give the vector equation directly:

Mq¨+Cq˙+Kq=Bx,y=Lq.M\ddot q+C\dot q+Kq=Bx,\qquad y=Lq.Mq¨​+Cq˙​+Kq=Bx,y=Lq.
(2.7)

2.4What the matrices mean

Symmetry. The equality qTAq=qTATqq^TAq=q^TA^TqqTAq=qTATq shows that only the symmetric part contributes to a quadratic form. The energy model gives symmetric MMM and KKK. Assumption A2 specifies a symmetric CCC.

Definiteness. A matrix AAA is positive semidefinite if xTAx≥0x^TAx\ge0xTAx≥0. It is positive definite if xTAx>0x^TAx>0xTAx>0 for all x≠0x\ne0x=0. Here T≥0T\ge0T≥0, and T=0T=0T=0 only when q˙=0\dot q=0q˙​=0. Thus M≻0M\succ0M≻0 and MMM is invertible. The strain energy V≥0V\ge0V≥0. A restrained structure has K≻0K\succ0K≻0. A free-free structure has K⪰0K\succeq0K⪰0 and rigid-body modes with Kϕ=0K\phi=0Kϕ=0. Also D≥0D\ge0D≥0, so C⪰0C\succeq0C⪰0. The damping matrix can be singular.

Units. Let qqq be in meters and xxx in newtons. Then MMM is in kilograms, CCC is in newton-seconds per meter, and KKK is in newtons per meter. Each term in (2.7) is a force. The matrices BBB and LLL account for input and sensor units.

Two masses. Consider masses m1m_1m1​ and m2m_2m2​. Spring k1k_1k1​ and damper c1c_1c1​ connect the wall to m1m_1m1​. Spring k2k_2k2​ and damper c2c_2c2​ connect the masses. Spring k3k_3k3​ and damper c3c_3c3​ connect m2m_2m2​ to the wall. Let q=[q1,q2]Tq=[q_1,q_2]^Tq=[q1​,q2​]T. Then:

M=[m100m2],K=[k1+k2−k2−k2k2+k3],C=[c1+c2−c2−c2c2+c3].M=\begin{bmatrix}m_1&0\\0&m_2\end{bmatrix},\qquad K=\begin{bmatrix}k_1+k_2&-k_2\\-k_2&k_2+k_3\end{bmatrix},\qquad C=\begin{bmatrix}c_1+c_2&-c_2\\-c_2&c_2+c_3\end{bmatrix}.M=[m1​0​0m2​​],K=[k1​+k2​−k2​​−k2​k2​+k3​​],C=[c1​+c2​−c2​​−c2​c2​+c3​​].
(2.8)

The off-diagonal entries are negative. The spring and damper between the masses oppose their relative motion. The energy terms are:

V=12[k1q12+k2(q2−q1)2+k3q22],D=12[c1q˙12+c2(q˙2−q˙1)2+c3q˙22].V=\tfrac12\left[k_1q_1^2+k_2(q_2-q_1)^2+k_3q_2^2\right],\qquad D=\tfrac12\left[c_1\dot q_1^2+c_2(\dot q_2-\dot q_1)^2+c_3\dot q_2^2\right].V=21​[k1​q12​+k2​(q2​−q1​)2+k3​q22​],D=21​[c1​q˙​12​+c2​(q˙​2​−q˙​1​)2+c3​q˙​22​].

Each bracket is a sum of squares with positive coefficients. Thus V,D≥0V,D\ge0V,D≥0. The matrix K≻0K\succ0K≻0 when k1+k2>0k_1+k_2>0k1​+k2​>0 and k1k2+k1k3+k2k3>0k_1k_2+k_1k_3+k_2k_3>0k1​k2​+k1​k3​+k2​k3​>0. These conditions hold for positive springs. A force on m1m_1m1​ gives B=[1,0]TB=[1,0]^TB=[1,0]T. If both displacements are measured, L=IL=IL=I.

2.5Lagrange’s equations for the matrix case

Use qqq as the generalized coordinate and Q=BxQ=BxQ=Bx as the generalized force:

ddt∂(T−V)∂q˙−∂(T−V)∂q+∂D∂q˙=Q.\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial (T-V)}{\partial\dot q}-\frac{\partial (T-V)}{\partial q}+\frac{\partial D}{\partial\dot q}=Q.dtd​∂q˙​∂(T−V)​−∂q∂(T−V)​+∂q˙​∂D​=Q.

3Modal analysis: free vibration

Free vibration is motion without an applied force. A mode is a spatial pattern that evolves at one complex rate.

3.1The exponential ansatz and the quadratic eigenproblem

Set x=0x=0x=0 in (2.7):

Mq¨+Cq˙+Kq=0.M\ddot q+C\dot q+Kq=0.Mq¨​+Cq˙​+Kq=0.

This linear equation has constant coefficients and exponential solutions. Repeated eigenvalues can also give polynomial factors. Assumption A5 excludes repeated eigenvalues. Use:

qc(t)=ϕeλt,q˙c=λϕeλt,q¨c=λ2ϕeλt.q_c(t)=\phi e^{\lambda t},\qquad \dot q_c=\lambda\phi e^{\lambda t},\qquad \ddot q_c=\lambda^2\phi e^{\lambda t}.qc​(t)=ϕeλt,q˙​c​=λϕeλt,q¨​c​=λ2ϕeλt.
(3.1)

The subscript ccc identifies a complex auxiliary solution. The nonzero vector ϕ\phiϕ is its spatial pattern. The scalar λ\lambdaλ is its complex rate. Substitute these terms into the free-vibration equation:

(λ2M+λC+K)ϕ eλt=0.\left(\lambda^2M+\lambda C+K\right)\phi\,e^{\lambda t}=0.(λ2M+λC+K)ϕeλt=0.

Cancel the exponential term and define:

Z(s)=s2M+sC+K,Z(λ)ϕ=0,det⁡Z(λ)=0.Z(s)=s^2M+sC+K,\qquad Z(\lambda)\phi=0,\qquad \det Z(\lambda)=0.Z(s)=s2M+sC+K,Z(λ)ϕ=0,detZ(λ)=0.
(3.2)

The nonzero vector ϕ\phiϕ makes Z(λ)Z(\lambda)Z(λ) singular. A zero determinant gives a null vector. The scale of ϕ\phiϕ is arbitrary; its direction gives the shape. This is a quadratic eigenvalue problem. The leading term of det⁡Z(s)\det Z(s)detZ(s) is det⁡(M)s2n\det(M)s^{2n}det(M)s2n. Thus the polynomial has degree 2n2n2n and has 2n2n2n roots. The real matrices give conjugate pairs. A numerical solver can use the 2n×2n2n\times2n2n×2n state form z=[q;q˙]z=[q;\dot q]z=[q;q˙​]. Its eigenvectors stack ϕm\phi_mϕm​ on λmϕm\lambda_m\phi_mλm​ϕm​. See Appendix A.

3.2Real motion from complex modes

The auxiliary solution qcq_cqc​ is complex, but the physical displacement qqq is real. The real matrices also give the conjugate pair λˉ\bar\lambdaλˉ and ϕˉ\bar\phiϕˉ​. Combine the pair:

qm(t)=c ϕeλt+cˉ ϕˉeλˉt=2Re⁡ ⁣(c ϕeλt).q_m(t)=c\,\phi e^{\lambda t}+\bar c\,\bar\phi e^{\bar\lambda t}=2\operatorname{Re}\!\left(c\,\phi e^{\lambda t}\right).qm​(t)=cϕeλt+cˉϕˉ​eλˉt=2Re(cϕeλt).
(3.3)

Part IIFrom forces to spectra

4The transfer matrix and its residues

Free vibration gives the poles. The transfer matrix maps forces to sensor measurements in the frequency domain. Its residues describe the contribution of each pole.

4.1The Laplace transform

For a signal q(t)q(t)q(t) on t≥0t\ge0t≥0, define the Laplace transform:

Q(s)=L{q}(s)=∫0∞q(t)e−st dt,s=σ+jω.Q(s)=\mathcal L\{q\}(s)=\int_0^\infty q(t)e^{-st}\,dt,\qquad s=\sigma+j\omega.Q(s)=L{q}(s)=∫0∞​q(t)e−stdt,s=σ+jω.
(4.1)

This is the Fourier transform of q(t)e−σtq(t)e^{-\sigma t}q(t)e−σt. Choose σ\sigmaσ large enough for the integral to converge. Integration by parts gives the derivative rule. Use u=e−stu=e^{-st}u=e−st and dv=q˙ dtdv=\dot q\,dtdv=q˙​dt:

∫0∞q˙(t)e−st dt=[q(t)e−st]0∞+s∫0∞q(t)e−st dt=sQ(s)−q(0).\int_0^\infty\dot q(t)e^{-st}\,dt=\bigl[q(t)e^{-st}\bigr]_0^\infty+s\int_0^\infty q(t)e^{-st}\,dt=sQ(s)-q(0).∫0∞​q˙​(t)e−stdt=[q(t)e−st]0∞​+s∫0∞​q(t)e−stdt=sQ(s)−q(0).

The upper limit is zero for the selected σ\sigmaσ. The lower limit gives −q(0)-q(0)−q(0). Apply the rule again:

L{q˙}(s)=sQ(s)−q(0),L{q¨}(s)=s2Q(s)−sq(0)−q˙(0).\mathcal L\{\dot q\}(s)=sQ(s)-q(0),\qquad \mathcal L\{\ddot q\}(s)=s^2Q(s)-sq(0)-\dot q(0).L{q˙​}(s)=sQ(s)−q(0),L{q¨​}(s)=s2Q(s)−sq(0)−q˙​(0).
(4.2)

For zero initial conditions, each time derivative becomes multiplication by sss. The initial-condition response can be added separately. On the imaginary axis, s=jω=j2πfs=j\omega=j2\pi fs=jω=j2πf, the transfer function gives the frequency response.

4.2From the equation of motion to H(s)H(s)H(s)

Apply the Laplace transform to (2.7) with zero initial conditions:

(s2M+sC+K)⏟Z(s)Q(s)=BX(s),Y(s)=LQ(s).\underbrace{(s^2M+sC+K)}_{Z(s)}Q(s)=BX(s),\qquad Y(s)=LQ(s).Z(s)(s2M+sC+K)​​Q(s)=BX(s),Y(s)=LQ(s).
(4.3)

When Z(s)Z(s)Z(s) is invertible:

Q(s)=Z(s)−1BX(s),Y(s)=LZ(s)−1BX(s),Q(s)=Z(s)^{-1}BX(s),\qquad Y(s)=LZ(s)^{-1}BX(s),Q(s)=Z(s)−1BX(s),Y(s)=LZ(s)−1BX(s),

so

Y(s)=H(s)X(s),H(s)=LZ(s)−1B.Y(s)=H(s)X(s),\qquad H(s)=LZ(s)^{-1}B.Y(s)=H(s)X(s),H(s)=LZ(s)−1B.
(4.4)

The transfer matrix HHH has size p×rp\times rp×r. Entry HikH_{ik}Hik​ maps input kkk to sensor iii. Its entries have a common denominator, det⁡Z(s)\det Z(s)detZ(s). The matrix ZZZ is singular at the eigenvalues. A pole can cancel if the input or output map does not couple to that mode.

4.3Partial fractions at a simple pole

For one entry with a simple pole at λm\lambda_mλm​, write:

Hik(s)=rik,ms−λm+gik,m(s),H_{ik}(s)=\frac{r_{ik,m}}{s-\lambda_m}+g_{ik,m}(s),Hik​(s)=s−λm​rik,m​​+gik,m​(s),
(4.5)

The remainder gik,mg_{ik,m}gik,m​ is finite at λm\lambda_mλm​. This separation is exact. Multiply by s−λms-\lambda_ms−λm​ and take the limit:

lim⁡s→λm(s−λm)Hik(s)=lim⁡s→λm[rik,m+(s−λm)gik,m(s)]=rik,m.\lim_{s\to\lambda_m}(s-\lambda_m)H_{ik}(s)=\lim_{s\to\lambda_m}\left[r_{ik,m}+(s-\lambda_m)g_{ik,m}(s)\right]=r_{ik,m}.s→λm​lim​(s−λm​)Hik​(s)=s→λm​lim​[rik,m​+(s−λm​)gik,m​(s)]=rik,m​.

H(s)=Rms−λm+Hrest,m(s),Rm=lim⁡s→λm(s−λm)H(s).H(s)=\frac{R_m}{s-\lambda_m}+H_{\mathrm{rest},m}(s),\qquad R_m=\lim_{s\to\lambda_m}(s-\lambda_m)H(s).H(s)=s−λm​Rm​​+Hrest,m​(s),Rm​=s→λm​lim​(s−λm​)H(s).

The residue RmR_mRm​ has size p×rp\times rp×r. The remainder Hrest,mH_{\mathrm{rest},m}Hrest,m​ contains the conjugate pole and all other modes. For a simple pole (A5), the principal part has one term.

4.4Why the residue is rank one

Separate the transfer from force to coordinates from the sensor map:

T(s)=Z(s)−1B,Q(s)=T(s)X(s),H(s)=LT(s).\mathcal T(s)=Z(s)^{-1}B,\qquad Q(s)=\mathcal T(s)X(s),\qquad H(s)=L\mathcal T(s).T(s)=Z(s)−1B,Q(s)=T(s)X(s),H(s)=LT(s).

Let WmW_mWm​ be the residue of T\mathcal TT at λm\lambda_mλm​:

Wm=lim⁡s→λm(s−λm)T(s).W_m=\lim_{s\to\lambda_m}(s-\lambda_m)\mathcal T(s).Wm​=s→λm​lim​(s−λm​)T(s).

Multiply Z(s)T(s)=BZ(s)\mathcal T(s)=BZ(s)T(s)=B by s−λms-\lambda_ms−λm​ and take the limit:

Z(λm)Wm=lim⁡s→λm(s−λm)B=0.Z(\lambda_m)W_m=\lim_{s\to\lambda_m}(s-\lambda_m)B=0.Z(λm​)Wm​=s→λm​lim​(s−λm​)B=0.
(4.7)

Each column of WmW_mWm​ is in the nullspace of Z(λm)Z(\lambda_m)Z(λm​). The nullspace contains the vectors that Z(λm)Z(\lambda_m)Z(λm​) maps to zero. At a simple eigenvalue, that nullspace has one dimension. Thus each column is a multiple of ϕm\phi_mϕm​. Let γm,k\gamma_{m,k}γm,k​ be the scalar for input kkk:

Wm=[ϕmγm,1⋯ϕmγm,r]=ϕmγmT,γmT=[γm,1⋯γm,r].W_m=\begin{bmatrix}\phi_m\gamma_{m,1}&\cdots&\phi_m\gamma_{m,r}\end{bmatrix}=\phi_m\gamma_m^T,\qquad \gamma_m^T=\begin{bmatrix}\gamma_{m,1}&\cdots&\gamma_{m,r}\end{bmatrix}.Wm​=[ϕm​γm,1​​⋯​ϕm​γm,r​​]=ϕm​γmT​,γmT​=[γm,1​​⋯​γm,r​​].

The matrix LLL is constant. Apply it to the limit:

Rm=lim⁡s→λm(s−λm)H(s)=Llim⁡s→λm(s−λm)T(s)=LWm=(Lϕm)γmT=vmγmT.R_m=\lim_{s\to\lambda_m}(s-\lambda_m)H(s)=L\lim_{s\to\lambda_m}(s-\lambda_m)\mathcal T(s)=LW_m=(L\phi_m)\gamma_m^T=v_m\gamma_m^T.Rm​=s→λm​lim​(s−λm​)H(s)=Ls→λm​lim​(s−λm​)T(s)=LWm​=(Lϕm​)γmT​=vm​γmT​.
(4.8)

The residue has rank at most one: each column is a multiple of the measured shape vmv_mvm​. If vm=0v_m=0vm​=0, the sensors do not see the mode. If γm=0\gamma_m=0γm​=0, the inputs do not excite it. In either case the residue is zero.

For example, let two input coefficients be 222 and −3-3−3, and let vm=[1,−2]Tv_m=[1,-2]^Tvm​=[1,−2]T:

Rm=[2vm−3vm]=[2−3−46]=[1−2][2−3].R_m=\begin{bmatrix}2v_m&-3v_m\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2&-3\\-4&6\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\-2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2&-3\end{bmatrix}.Rm​=[2vm​​−3vm​​]=[2−4​−36​]=[1−2​][2​−3​].

Both columns keep the ratio 1:−21:-21:−2. An input vector combines them into vm(2X1−3X2)v_m(2X_1-3X_2)vm​(2X1​−3X2​). The full transfer matrix contains the other modes and need not have rank one. The rank statement applies to one residue.

4.5The full modal sum

For real matrices, the conjugate pole has residue Rˉm\bar R_mRˉm​. Sum the nnn pairs:

H(s)=∑m=1n(Rms−λm+Rˉms−λˉm),Rm=vmγmT.H(s)=\sum_{m=1}^{n}\left(\frac{R_m}{s-\lambda_m}+\frac{\bar R_m}{s-\bar\lambda_m}\right),\qquad R_m=v_m\gamma_m^T.H(s)=m=1∑n​(s−λm​Rm​​+s−λˉm​Rˉm​​),Rm​=vm​γmT​.
(4.9)

This sum is exact under A5. It does not assume that one mode dominates. A zero vmv_mvm​, zero γm\gamma_mγm​, or cancellation removes a term from HHH. The mode still exists.

5The response spectral matrix

Operational forces are unknown and can vary between records. The spectral matrix is an average of products of Fourier coefficients.

5.1From records to a spectral matrix

Let TTT be the record duration and y(t)y(t)y(t) the measurement from ppp channels. Define:

YT(f)=∫−T/2T/2y(t)e−j2πft dt,Gy(f)=lim⁡T→∞1TE ⁣[YT(f)YT(f)H].Y_T(f)=\int_{-T/2}^{T/2}y(t)e^{-j2\pi ft}\,dt,\qquad G_y(f)=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\mathbb E\!\left[Y_T(f)Y_T(f)^H\right].YT​(f)=∫−T/2T/2​y(t)e−j2πftdt,Gy​(f)=T→∞lim​T1​E[YT​(f)YT​(f)H].
(5.1)

The transform YTY_TYT​ is random. The operator E\mathbb EE denotes an average over records. Entry (i,k)(i,k)(i,k) of YTYTHY_TY_T^HYT​YTH​ is YiYˉkY_i\bar Y_kYi​Yˉk​. The factor 1/T1/T1/T gives a density in amplitude squared per hertz. The integral of a diagonal entry over all frequencies gives the channel mean square. It equals the variance when the mean is zero.

This is a two-sided spectral matrix. For real signals, negative frequencies mirror positive frequencies. A one-sided spectrum is marked +^++. It doubles interior positive bins but does not double DC or Nyquist. Assumption A6 specifies wide-sense stationarity and a spectral density. The expected products then depend only on time separation. Ergodicity permits a time average to estimate the ensemble average. See Appendix D for estimation details.

5.2Hermitian positive semidefiniteness

For any YYY,

(YYH)H=(YH)HYH=YYH.\left(YY^H\right)^H=\left(Y^H\right)^HY^H=YY^H.(YYH)H=(YH)HYH=YYH.

A matrix is Hermitian if it equals its conjugate transpose. Expectation preserves this property, so GyG_yGy​ is Hermitian. Its diagonal entries are averages of ∣Yi∣2|Y_i|^2∣Yi​∣2. They are real and nonnegative. For any complex weight vector aaa, ∣aHYT∣2≥0|a^HY_T|^2\ge0∣aHYT​∣2≥0. The average gives:

GyH=Gy,aHGya=lim⁡T→∞1TE ⁣[∣aHYT∣2]≥0.G_y^H=G_y,\qquad a^HG_ya=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\mathbb E\!\left[|a^HY_T|^2\right]\ge0.GyH​=Gy​,aHGy​a=T→∞lim​T1​E[∣aHYT​∣2]≥0.
(5.2)

Thus GyG_yGy​ is Hermitian positive semidefinite. The spectral theorem gives an orthonormal eigenbasis and real eigenvalues. Positive semidefiniteness makes those eigenvalues nonnegative. With unitary UUU and diagonal Λ\LambdaΛ:

Gy=UΛUH,UHU=I,Λ=diag⁡(λ1,…,λp),λk≥0.G_y=U\Lambda U^H,\qquad U^HU=I,\qquad \Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_p),\quad \lambda_k\ge0.Gy​=UΛUH,UHU=I,Λ=diag(λ1​,…,λp​),λk​≥0.

For this matrix, the singular values are the eigenvalues. The left singular vectors are eigenvectors. The rank is the number of nonzero eigenvalues. A rank-one p×pp\times pp×p matrix has one nonzero eigenvalue and a nullspace of dimension p−1p-1p−1.

5.3The input–output relation

For a sufficiently long record of the stationary forced response, the Fourier-domain relation is approximately:

YT(f)≈H(j2πf)XT(f).Y_T(f)\approx H(j2\pi f)X_T(f).YT​(f)≈H(j2πf)XT​(f).

This approximation follows from (4.4) after transients decay. For finite records, boundary effects generally prevent exact equality. Substitute the approximate relation into the outer product:

YTYTH≈(HXT)(HXT)H=HXTXTHHH.Y_TY_T^H\approx\left(HX_T\right)\left(HX_T\right)^H=HX_TX_T^HH^H.YT​YTH​≈(HXT​)(HXT​)H=HXT​XTH​HH.

At a fixed frequency, HHH is constant across realizations. It can therefore pass through the expectation. Apply (5.1) in the infinite-record limit:

Gy(f)=H(j2πf) Gx(f) H(j2πf)H.G_y(f)=H(j2\pi f)\,G_x(f)\,H(j2\pi f)^H.Gy​(f)=H(j2πf)Gx​(f)H(j2πf)H.
(5.3)

The input spectral matrix GxG_xGx​ has size r×rr\times rr×r. It is Hermitian positive semidefinite. The output spectral matrix GyG_yGy​ has size p×pp\times pp×p. The matrix GxG_xGx​ describes the excitation. The transfer matrix HHH describes the structural response and the sensors.

5.4Conventions and estimation

This page defines entry (i,k)(i,k)(i,k) as YiYˉkY_i\bar Y_kYi​Yˉk​. Some software uses YˉiYk\bar Y_iY_kYˉi​Yk​. That convention gives the transpose and conjugate of this matrix, and the estimated shape is conjugated. Do not mix the two conventions. A one-sided spectrum keeps f≥0f\ge0f≥0 and doubles the interior bins. Its integral matches the two-sided mean square. Do not double DC or Nyquist. See Appendix D for the Welch estimator, its normalization, and the resolution–variance tradeoff.

Part IIIFinding modes in data

6When one mode dominates

The response matrix contains rank-one terms and their cross terms. FDD uses a frequency band where one term dominates. This section separates that term and gives a bound for the other terms.

6.1Isolating one pole

Let s=jωs=j\omegas=jω on the imaginary axis, where ω=2πf\omega=2\pi fω=2πf. Separate mode mmm:

H(jω)=Rmjω−λm+Em(jω),Rm=vmγmT.H(j\omega)=\frac{R_m}{j\omega-\lambda_m}+E_m(j\omega),\qquad R_m=v_m\gamma_m^T.H(jω)=jω−λm​Rm​​+Em​(jω),Rm​=vm​γmT​.
(6.1)

The remainder EmE_mEm​ contains the conjugate pole and all other modes. It is finite at ωd,m\omega_{d,m}ωd,m​ (A5). The selected denominator is

jω−λm=αm+j(ω−ωd,m),∣jω−λm∣2=αm2+(ω−ωd,m)2.j\omega-\lambda_m=\alpha_m+j(\omega-\omega_{d,m}),\qquad |j\omega-\lambda_m|^2=\alpha_m^2+(\omega-\omega_{d,m})^2.jω−λm​=αm​+j(ω−ωd,m​),∣jω−λm​∣2=αm2​+(ω−ωd,m​)2.

At ω=ωd,m\omega=\omega_{d,m}ω=ωd,m​, the magnitude of the denominator is αm\alpha_mαm​. Thus, the selected term grows as 1/αm1/\alpha_m1/αm​. The remainder has no such denominator.

6.2The exact four-term expansion

Let P=Rm/(jω−λm)P=R_m/(j\omega-\lambda_m)P=Rm​/(jω−λm​) and E=EmE=E_mE=Em​. Substitute these terms into (5.3):

Gy=(P+E)Gx(P+E)H=PGxPH+PGxEH+EGxPH+EGxEH.G_y=(P+E)G_x(P+E)^H=PG_xP^H+PG_xE^H+EG_xP^H+EG_xE^H.Gy​=(P+E)Gx​(P+E)H=PGx​PH+PGx​EH+EGx​PH+EGx​EH.
(6.2)

This expansion is exact. The first term contains the selected pole twice. The two middle terms combine the selected pole with the remainder. The last term contains the remainder twice. Since PH=RmH/(−jω−λˉm)P^H=R_m^H/(-j\omega-\bar\lambda_m)PH=RmH​/(−jω−λˉm​),

PGxPH=RmGxRmH∣jω−λm∣2.PG_xP^H=\frac{R_mG_xR_m^H}{|j\omega-\lambda_m|^2}.PGx​PH=∣jω−λm​∣2Rm​Gx​RmH​​.

With RmH=γˉmvmHR_m^H=\bar\gamma_mv_m^HRmH​=γˉ​m​vmH​,

RmGxRmH=vmγmTGxγˉm vmH=(γmTGxγˉm)vmvmH.R_mG_xR_m^H=v_m\gamma_m^TG_x\bar\gamma_m\,v_m^H=\left(\gamma_m^TG_x\bar\gamma_m\right)v_mv_m^H.Rm​Gx​RmH​=vm​γmT​Gx​γˉ​m​vmH​=(γmT​Gx​γˉ​m​)vm​vmH​.

Define the scalar weight

Gy≈dm vmvmH,dm(f)=γmTGx(f)γˉmαm2+(2πf−ωd,m)2≥0.G_y\approx d_m\,v_mv_m^H,\qquad d_m(f)=\frac{\gamma_m^TG_x(f)\bar\gamma_m}{\alpha_m^2+(2\pi f-\omega_{d,m})^2}\ge0.Gy​≈dm​vm​vmH​,dm​(f)=αm2​+(2πf−ωd,m​)2γmT​Gx​(f)γˉ​m​​≥0.
(6.3)

The numerator is (γˉm)HGx(γˉm)≥0(\bar\gamma_m)^HG_x(\bar\gamma_m)\ge0(γˉ​m​)HGx​(γˉ​m​)≥0, because GxG_xGx​ is positive semidefinite. The direction vmv_mvm​ is constant. Only the weight dmd_mdm​ changes with frequency. If Gx≈QxG_x\approx Q_xGx​≈Qx​ is constant,

dm(f)=γmTQxγˉmαm2+(2πf−ωd,m)2,d_m(f)=\frac{\gamma_m^TQ_x\bar\gamma_m}{\alpha_m^2+(2\pi f-\omega_{d,m})^2},dm​(f)=αm2​+(2πf−ωd,m​)2γmT​Qx​γˉ​m​​,

This is a Lorentzian curve with a peak at ωd,m\omega_{d,m}ωd,m​. The numerator sets its height. The decay rate αm\alpha_mαm​ sets its width.

6.3The residual bound

You can omit the last three terms of (6.2) when they are small. Weight the selected term and the remainder by the excitation. Let Gx1/2G_x^{1/2}Gx1/2​ be the positive-semidefinite square root of GxG_xGx​:

Pw=PGx1/2,Ew=EGx1/2.P_w=PG_x^{1/2},\qquad E_w=EG_x^{1/2}.Pw​=PGx1/2​,Ew​=EGx1/2​.

Then PwPwH=PGxPHP_wP_w^H=PG_xP^HPw​PwH​=PGx​PH, PwEwH=PGxEHP_wE_w^H=PG_xE^HPw​EwH​=PGx​EH, EwPwH=EGxPHE_wP_w^H=EG_xP^HEw​PwH​=EGx​PH, EwEwH=EGxEHE_wE_w^H=EG_xE^HEw​EwH​=EGx​EH, so

Gy=PwPwH+PwEwH+EwPwH+EwEwH.G_y=P_wP_w^H+P_wE_w^H+E_wP_w^H+E_wE_w^H.Gy​=Pw​PwH​+Pw​EwH​+Ew​PwH​+Ew​EwH​.

With ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_2∥⋅∥2​ the spectral norm, the triangle inequality and ∥AB∥2≤∥A∥2∥B∥2\|AB\|_2\le\|A\|_2\|B\|_2∥AB∥2​≤∥A∥2​∥B∥2​ give

∥Gy−PwPwH∥2≤2∥Pw∥2∥Ew∥2+∥Ew∥22.\left\|G_y-P_wP_w^H\right\|_2\le2\|P_w\|_2\|E_w\|_2+\|E_w\|_2^2.​Gy​−Pw​PwH​​2​≤2∥Pw​∥2​∥Ew​∥2​+∥Ew​∥22​.
(6.4)

If ∥Ew∥2≤ε∥Pw∥2\|E_w\|_2\le\varepsilon\|P_w\|_2∥Ew​∥2​≤ε∥Pw​∥2​, then

∥Gy−PwPwH∥2≤(2ε+ε2)∥Pw∥22.\left\|G_y-P_wP_w^H\right\|_2\le(2\varepsilon+\varepsilon^2)\|P_w\|_2^2.​Gy​−Pw​PwH​​2​≤(2ε+ε2)∥Pw​∥22​.

The value of ε\varepsilonε depends on the force spectrum, modal visibility, and pole separation. It does not depend only on damping. A lightly damped mode can have a large ε\varepsilonε near a strongly excited mode. A heavily damped mode can have a small ε\varepsilonε if it is alone in the band. Appendix C gives the bound again.

6.4What the assumption really says

The assumption applies to the response in the selected band. In that band, the selected mode must dominate the response that the forces excite and the sensors measure. A mode can be invisible if vmv_mvm​ is small, for example when the sensors are near a node. It can also be invisible if γm\gamma_mγm​ is small, because the forces do not excite it sufficiently. Close modes increase EEE. A colored force spectrum can distort the weight and shift the peak. Correlated inputs matter when more than one mode contributes. Noise adds a full-rank term.

6.5Worked example: two sensors

Assume that one mode moves sensor 1 by 111 mm and sensor 2 by −2-2−2 mm. Let a(t)a(t)a(t) be the first displacement:

y(t)=[a(t)−2a(t)]=v a(t),v=[1−2].y(t)=\begin{bmatrix}a(t)\\-2a(t)\end{bmatrix}=v\,a(t),\qquad v=\begin{bmatrix}1\\-2\end{bmatrix}.y(t)=[a(t)−2a(t)​]=va(t),v=[1−2​].
(6.5)

Let A(f)A(f)A(f) be the Fourier coefficient of aaa. By linearity, Y1=AY_1=AY1​=A and Y2=−2AY_2=-2AY2​=−2A. Thus,

∣Y1∣2=∣A∣2,∣Y2∣2=4∣A∣2,Y1Yˉ2=−2∣A∣2.|Y_1|^2=|A|^2,\qquad |Y_2|^2=4|A|^2,\qquad Y_1\bar Y_2=-2|A|^2.∣Y1​∣2=∣A∣2,∣Y2​∣2=4∣A∣2,Y1​Yˉ2​=−2∣A∣2.

The separate power spectra do not show the sign. The cross product shows that the sensors move in opposite directions. Average and normalize the products:

Gy(f)=Sa(f) vvT=Sa(f)[1−2−24],G_y(f)=S_a(f)\,vv^T=S_a(f)\begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\-2&4\end{bmatrix},Gy​(f)=Sa​(f)vvT=Sa​(f)[1−2​−24​],
(6.6)

where SaS_aSa​ is the PSD of aaa. For Sa>0S_a>0Sa​>0 the matrix is rank one, and

Gyv=5Sa(f) v,Gy[21]=0.G_yv=5S_a(f)\,v,\qquad G_y\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}=0.Gy​v=5Sa​(f)v,Gy​[21​]=0.
(6.7)

The eigenvalue depends on excitation strength. The eigenvector gives the relative motion 1:−21:-21:−2. The null vector [2,1]T[2,1]^T[2,1]T is orthogonal to vvv. The shape has an arbitrary scale and phase. Where Sa=0S_a=0Sa​=0, there is no preferred direction. FDD therefore estimates shapes at peaks.

7Frequency domain decomposition

FDD diagonalizes the measured spectral matrix at each frequency. This decomposition is exact. The interpretation of the leading vector as a mode shape uses the approximation in §6.

7.1The SVD at each frequency

At frequency fif_ifi​, diagonalize the estimate G^y\widehat G_yGy​:

G^y(fi)=UiSiUiH=∑k=1psk(fi) uk(fi)uk(fi)H,s1≥s2≥⋯≥sp≥0.\widehat G_y(f_i)=U_iS_iU_i^H=\sum_{k=1}^{p}s_k(f_i)\,u_k(f_i)u_k(f_i)^H,\qquad s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots\ge s_p\ge0.Gy​(fi​)=Ui​Si​UiH​=k=1∑p​sk​(fi​)uk​(fi​)uk​(fi​)H,s1​≥s2​≥⋯≥sp​≥0.
(7.1)

The columns of UiU_iUi​ are orthonormal eigenvectors. The matrix SiS_iSi​ is diagonal. For a Hermitian positive-semidefinite matrix, the SVD and eigendecomposition give the same result. The singular values are the eigenvalues. The left singular vectors are the eigenvectors. The first term is the largest.

An exact rank-one matrix has only s1≠0s_1\ne0s1​=0. Other modes, noise, and finite-record errors usually make the estimate full rank. For u1u_1u1​ to be close to the physical shape, s2s_2s2​ must be sufficiently small. See Appendix E.

7.2The leading singular vector

For G≈d vvHG\approx d\,vv^HG≈dvvH with v≠0v\ne0v=0,

(d vvH)v=d ∥v∥2 v,\left(d\,vv^H\right)v=d\,\|v\|^2\,v,(dvvH)v=d∥v∥2v,
(7.2)

so vvv is an eigenvector with eigenvalue d∥v∥2d\|v\|^2d∥v∥2. Normalizing,

u1≈ejθv∥v∥,s1≈d ∥v∥2.u_1\approx e^{j\theta}\frac{v}{\|v\|},\qquad s_1\approx d\,\|v\|^2.u1​≈ejθ∥v∥v​,s1​≈d∥v∥2.
(7.3)

The phase θ\thetaθ is arbitrary. You can multiply vvv by a constant and adjust ddd without changing d vvHd\,vv^HdvvH. The absolute scale and phase are therefore unknown. Modal mass is not identifiable from this result. For G=G0+EG=G_0+EG=G0​+E, with G0=d vvHG_0=d\,vv^HG0​=dvvH, the leading vector is close to v/∥v∥v/\|v\|v/∥v∥ when ∥E∥2\|E\|_2∥E∥2​ is small relative to the spectral gap. See the bound in Appendix E. A large s1/s2s_1/s_2s1​/s2​ supports a well-defined direction. A ratio near one does not. For the two-sensor example, u1=[1,−2]T/5u_1=[1,-2]^T/\sqrt5u1​=[1,−2]T/5​ and s1=5Sas_1=5S_as1​=5Sa​.

7.3Peak frequency is not pole frequency

The spectral peak of a single oscillator can differ from ωn\omega_nωn​ and ωd\omega_dωd​. Omit the subscripts. The force-to-displacement transfer function is

h(jω)=1ωn2−ω2+j2ζωnω,h(j\omega)=\frac{1}{\omega_n^2-\omega^2+j2\zeta\omega_n\omega},h(jω)=ωn2​−ω2+j2ζωn​ω1​,

so

∣h(jω)∣2=1(ωn2−ω2)2+4ζ2ωn2ω2.\left|h(j\omega)\right|^2=\frac{1}{(\omega_n^2-\omega^2)^2+4\zeta^2\omega_n^2\omega^2}.∣h(jω)∣2=(ωn2​−ω2)2+4ζ2ωn2​ω21​.
(7.4)

Under white forcing the displacement PSD has the same frequency dependence. Minimize the denominator D(ω)D(\omega)D(ω):

D′(ω)=2(ωn2−ω2)(−2ω)+8ζ2ωn2ω=4ω[ω2−ωn2+2ζ2ωn2].D'(\omega)=2(\omega_n^2-\omega^2)(-2\omega)+8\zeta^2\omega_n^2\omega=4\omega\left[\omega^2-\omega_n^2+2\zeta^2\omega_n^2\right].D′(ω)=2(ωn2​−ω2)(−2ω)+8ζ2ωn2​ω=4ω[ω2−ωn2​+2ζ2ωn2​].

The stationary points are ω=0\omega=0ω=0 and ω2=ωn2(1−2ζ2)\omega^2=\omega_n^2(1-2\zeta^2)ω2=ωn2​(1−2ζ2). If ζ<1/2\zeta<1/\sqrt2ζ<1/2​, the positive root gives a minimum of DDD and a maximum of ∣h∣2|h|^2∣h∣2. If ζ≥1/2\zeta\ge1/\sqrt2ζ≥1/2​, the maximum occurs at ω=0\omega=0ω=0. Thus,

ωpeak=ωn1−2ζ2(ζ<1/2),ωpeak=0(ζ≥1/2).\omega_{\mathrm{peak}}=\omega_n\sqrt{1-2\zeta^2}\quad(\zeta<1/\sqrt2),\qquad \omega_{\mathrm{peak}}=0\quad(\zeta\ge1/\sqrt2).ωpeak​=ωn​1−2ζ2​(ζ<1/2​),ωpeak​=0(ζ≥1/2​).
(7.5)

For light damping, the three frequencies are close. For 0<ζ<1/20<\zeta<1/\sqrt20<ζ<1/2​, ωpeak<ωd<ωn\omega_{\mathrm{peak}}<\omega_d<\omega_nωpeak​<ωd​<ωn​. Colored forcing, acceleration measurement, and finite resolution can shift the measured peak. An acceleration PSD has an additional factor of ω4\omega^4ω4, which biases the peak upward.

7.4Two modes in one band

For two modes,

Gy=d1v1v1H+d2v2v2H.G_y=d_1v_1v_1^H+d_2v_2v_2^H.Gy​=d1​v1​v1H​+d2​v2​v2H​.
(7.6)

If v1Hv2=0v_1^Hv_2=0v1H​v2​=0, the eigenvectors are exactly v1,v2v_1,v_2v1​,v2​, with eigenvalues d1∥v1∥2,d2∥v2∥2d_1\|v_1\|^2,d_2\|v_2\|^2d1​∥v1​∥2,d2​∥v2​∥2. Otherwise

Gyv1=d1∥v1∥2v1+d2v2(v2Hv1),G_yv_1=d_1\|v_1\|^2v_1+d_2v_2\left(v_2^Hv_1\right),Gy​v1​=d1​∥v1​∥2v1​+d2​v2​(v2H​v1​),
(7.7)

The second term points away from v1v_1v1​. Thus, v1v_1v1​ is not an eigenvector and the leading vector is a mixture. If d1,d2>0d_1,d_2>0d1​,d2​>0 and v1,v2v_1,v_2v1​,v2​ are independent, GyG_yGy​ maps into their two-dimensional span. The first two singular vectors recover this span, but not the individual shapes. Orthogonal measured shapes are a special case. Mass-orthogonal physical modes do not necessarily give orthogonal measured shapes, because LLL does not preserve the mass inner product. If the singular values are equal, the basis within the subspace is not unique.

The modal assurance criterion measures agreement:

MAC⁡(u,v)=∣uHv∣2(uHu)(vHv)∈[0,1].\operatorname{MAC}(u,v)=\frac{|u^Hv|^2}{(u^Hu)(v^Hv)}\in[0,1].MAC(u,v)=(uHu)(vHv)∣uHv∣2​∈[0,1].
(7.8)

The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives a value between zero and one. The value is one for proportional vectors and zero for orthogonal vectors. It does not change when you scale either vector by a nonzero complex number. Use MAC to compare directions at adjacent frequencies.

7.5The algorithm

FDD, step by step

  1. Acquire. Record ppp synchronized channels with known units and orientations; choose segment length, window, and overlap.
  2. Estimate. Compute G^y(fi)\widehat G_y(f_i)Gy​(fi​) for every bin, using the same segments and window for all channel pairs and enough independent segments.
  3. Decompose. Diagonalize at each fif_ifi​ (7.1); store the singular values and leading vectors.
  4. Find peaks. Plot s1(f)s_1(f)s1​(f); a local maximum is a candidate resonance.
  5. Read the shape. At a peak take u1u_1u1​; check that s1/s2s_1/s_2s1​/s2​ is large and u1u_1u1​ is stable across bins by MAC.
  6. Estimate damping. If needed, select the bell around the peak by MAC and fit its correlation decay (§8).

Output. A candidate peak frequency and a shape u1u_1u1​, with arbitrary scale and phase. EFDD can also estimate the damped frequency fd,mf_{d,m}fd,m​ and damping ratio ζm\zeta_mζm​.

The eigendecomposition costs O(Nfp3)O(N_fp^3)O(Nf​p3) for NfN_fNf​ bins and ppp channels. This cost is small when ppp is small. The spectral estimate costs O(Nlog⁡N)O(N\log N)O(NlogN) per segment. Sensor placement and spectral settings require careful selection.

8Estimating damping: EFDD

FDD gives an estimate of shape and peak frequency. EFDD uses the width of the spectral peak to estimate damping. Select the part of the peak that belongs to one mode. Then inverse-transform it and fit the decay of its correlation.

8.1Selecting the spectral bell

Use the leading vector near a peak as the reference v^m\hat v_mv^m​. At each adjacent frequency, calculate MAC⁡(uk(f),v^m)\operatorname{MAC}(u_k(f),\hat v_m)MAC(uk​(f),v^m​). Keep a bin if its MAC exceeds the threshold. The selected bins form the spectral bell. A threshold of 0.80.80.8 is a common starting point. Track the direction by MAC. Do not rely on vector index, because the first and second singular vectors can cross. Set the rejected bins to zero. Examine the bell for asymmetry or roughness, which can indicate contamination.

The selected spectrum b+(f)b^+(f)b+(f) is one-sided. Its value at kΔfk\Delta fkΔf is b+[k]b^+[k]b+[k]. Appendix D defines the +^++ scaling. Double the interior bins, but do not double DC or Nyquist.

8.2From the bell to a correlation decay

The Wiener–Khinchin relation gives autocorrelation as the inverse transform of the PSD. For a real, even correlation, the result is a cosine integral:

Rm(τ)=∫0∞b+(f)cos⁡(2πfτ) df≈Δf∑k=0N/2b+[k]cos⁡ ⁣(2πkℓN),τ=ℓfs.\mathcal R_m(\tau)=\int_0^\infty b^+(f)\cos(2\pi f\tau)\,df\approx\Delta f\sum_{k=0}^{N/2}b^+[k]\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi k\ell}{N}\right),\qquad \tau=\frac{\ell}{f_s}.Rm​(τ)=∫0∞​b+(f)cos(2πfτ)df≈Δfk=0∑N/2​b+[k]cos(N2πkℓ​),τ=fs​ℓ​.
(8.1)

Here fsf_sfs​ is the sampling rate, NNN is an even transform length, Δf=fs/N\Delta f=f_s/NΔf=fs​/N, and ℓ\ellℓ is the lag index. The cosine comes from the mirrored negative frequencies. For a single mode, the correlation oscillates with the envelope am(τ)=A0e−αmτa_m(\tau)=A_0e^{-\alpha_m\tau}am​(τ)=A0​e−αm​τ, where A0>0A_0>0A0​>0. Its period is Td=2π/ωd,mT_d=2\pi/\omega_{d,m}Td​=2π/ωd,m​:

Rm(τ)∝am(τ)cos⁡(ωd,mτ),Td=2πωd,m.\mathcal R_m(\tau)\propto a_m(\tau)\cos(\omega_{d,m}\tau),\qquad T_d=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_{d,m}}.Rm​(τ)∝am​(τ)cos(ωd,m​τ),Td​=ωd,m​2π​.

8.3From log decrement to damping ratio

At two times separated by kkk periods, the envelope ratio is e−αmkTde^{-\alpha_mkT_d}e−αm​kTd​. The logarithm of this ratio per period is the logarithmic decrement:

δ=1kln⁡am(τ)am(τ+kTd)=αmTd.\delta=\frac{1}{k}\ln\frac{a_m(\tau)}{a_m(\tau+kT_d)}=\alpha_mT_d.δ=k1​lnam​(τ+kTd​)am​(τ)​=αm​Td​.
(8.2)

Substitute αm=ζmωn,m\alpha_m=\zeta_m\omega_{n,m}αm​=ζm​ωn,m​ and Td=2π/(ωn,m1−ζm2)T_d=2\pi/(\omega_{n,m}\sqrt{1-\zeta_m^2})Td​=2π/(ωn,m​1−ζm2​​); the natural frequency cancels:

δ=2πζm1−ζm2.\delta=\frac{2\pi\zeta_m}{\sqrt{1-\zeta_m^2}}.δ=1−ζm2​​2πζm​​.

Square and solve for ζm\zeta_mζm​:

δ2(1−ζm2)=4π2ζm2⟹ζm2=δ24π2+δ2⟹ζm=δ4π2+δ2,\delta^2(1-\zeta_m^2)=4\pi^2\zeta_m^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\zeta_m^2=\frac{\delta^2}{4\pi^2+\delta^2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\zeta_m=\frac{\delta}{\sqrt{4\pi^2+\delta^2}},δ2(1−ζm2​)=4π2ζm2​⟹ζm2​=4π2+δ2δ2​⟹ζm​=4π2+δ2​δ​,

taking the positive root. Then

ζm=δ4π2+δ2,fn,m=fd,m1−ζm2.\zeta_m=\frac{\delta}{\sqrt{4\pi^2+\delta^2}},\qquad f_{n,m}=\frac{f_{d,m}}{\sqrt{1-\zeta_m^2}}.ζm​=4π2+δ2​δ​,fn,m​=1−ζm2​​fd,m​​.
(8.3)

Fit a line to several peaks: ln⁡am(τj)=ln⁡A0−αmτj\ln a_m(\tau_j)=\ln A_0-\alpha_m\tau_jlnam​(τj​)=lnA0​−αm​τj​. The slope gives αm\alpha_mαm​. Peaks with the same sign are one period apart. Alternating extrema are half a period apart. Exclude the initial distorted part and the late noisy part.

8.4Practical bias

A nearby mode produces beating and can bias a single-exponential fit. A bell that is too narrow truncates the peak. A bell that is too wide includes neighboring modes and noise. Leakage changes the shape of the bell. Nonstationary excitation changes its height. Calculate damping for different bell widths and fitting intervals. A result that changes can indicate that the bell does not isolate one mode. Compare the EFDD frequency with (3.7) before you report it.

Part IVPractice

9Using the method on measurements

The checks below help you decide if the results are reliable.

9.1Before the measurement

  • Sensor placement. A sensor at a node records none of that mode. Place sensors where the target modes are large, and use enough to distinguish the shapes; vm=Lϕmv_m=L\phi_mvm​=Lϕm​ is limited by LLL.
  • Units and directions. Record the measured quantity, units, and positive direction. Arbitrary rescaling changes the geometry seen by the SVD; apply rotations before the spectral estimate.
  • Synchronization. All channels need one time base. A constant offset adds a frequency-dependent phase shift and corrupts the cross-spectra.
  • Stationarity. The excitation must be stationary over the record or each segment; transients, gusts, and operating changes violate A6.

9.2During spectral estimation

  • Same segments and window. Use them for every entry of G^y\widehat G_yGy​; otherwise the cross-channel phase is destroyed.
  • Enough averages. One segment gives a noisy estimate with artificially low rank. Overlap adds segments but not independent averages.
  • Resolution. Segment length sets resolution; zero-padding only densifies the grid. A peak narrower than the resolution cannot be separated from its neighbor.
  • Check stability. Plot s1(f)s_1(f)s1​(f) and s1/s2s_1/s_2s1​/s2​; a peak that moves with segment length or averaging is not stable.

9.3Interpreting the decomposition

  • Stable direction. The leading vector should be stable by MAC across the peak; rapid rotation means a mixture.
  • Rank one. A large s1/s2s_1/s_2s1​/s2​ supports the interpretation; a ratio near one leaves the direction undetermined.
  • Harmonic forcing. A sinusoid also gives a narrow rank-one peak. Check whether the frequency matches a known forcing frequency and whether the shape is structural.
  • Visibility. An absent peak does not prove an absent mode; it may be weakly excited or invisible at the sensors.
  • Nonlinearity. Harmonics, combination frequencies, and amplitude-dependent shapes violate the linear model.

9.4Reporting

Report the sensor coordinates, directions, measured quantity, and units. Report the shape normalization, phase convention, and cross-spectrum convention. Give the segment length, window, overlap, number of averages, and resolution. For EFDD, also report the bell, MAC threshold, and fit interval. State whether each frequency is damped fdf_dfd​ or natural fnf_nfn​. These frequencies differ by 1−ζ2\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}1−ζ2​. If a check fails, report the mixture or possible bias. Do not present the leading vector as a mode shape without qualification.

AState-space linearization

The quadratic eigenvalue problem (3.2) has an equivalent ordinary eigenproblem. The state vector includes displacement and velocity. Let zzz be the 2n2n2n-component state vector. Let III be the n×nn\times nn×n identity matrix. The zero blocks have the same size. The free equation Mq¨+Cq˙+Kq=0M\ddot q+C\dot q+Kq=0Mq¨​+Cq˙​+Kq=0 becomes

z=[qq˙],z˙=Az,A=[0I−M−1K−M−1C].z=\begin{bmatrix}q\\\dot q\end{bmatrix},\qquad \dot z=Az,\qquad A=\begin{bmatrix}0&I\\-M^{-1}K&-M^{-1}C\end{bmatrix}.z=[qq˙​​],z˙=Az,A=[0−M−1K​I−M−1C​].
(A.1)

The upper block of z˙=Az\dot z=Azz˙=Az gives the identity q˙=q˙\dot q=\dot qq˙​=q˙​. The lower block gives q¨=−M−1Kq−M−1Cq˙\ddot q=-M^{-1}Kq-M^{-1}C\dot qq¨​=−M−1Kq−M−1Cq˙​. This is the free equation multiplied by M−1M^{-1}M−1. The matrix AAA is 2n×2n2n\times2n2n×2n. Thus, it has 2n2n2n eigenvalues, with repeated roots counted by multiplicity. These are the eigenvalues of the quadratic problem, as the next calculation shows.

Let z=Ψeλtz=\Psi e^{\lambda t}z=Ψeλt be a state solution. Then z˙=λΨeλt\dot z=\lambda\Psi e^{\lambda t}z˙=λΨeλt. Cancellation of the exponential gives AΨ=λΨA\Psi=\lambda\PsiAΨ=λΨ. Let Ψ1\Psi_1Ψ1​ and Ψ2\Psi_2Ψ2​ be the upper and lower nnn-component blocks of Ψ\PsiΨ. The two block equations are

λΨ1=Ψ2,−M−1KΨ1−M−1CΨ2=λΨ2.\lambda\Psi_1=\Psi_2,\qquad -M^{-1}K\Psi_1-M^{-1}C\Psi_2=\lambda\Psi_2.λΨ1​=Ψ2​,−M−1KΨ1​−M−1CΨ2​=λΨ2​.
(A.2)

The first equation gives Ψ2=λΨ1\Psi_2=\lambda\Psi_1Ψ2​=λΨ1​. Substitute into the second and multiply by MMM:

−KΨ1−λCΨ1=λ2MΨ1⟹(λ2M+λC+K)Ψ1=0.-K\Psi_1-\lambda C\Psi_1=\lambda^2M\Psi_1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\left(\lambda^2M+\lambda C+K\right)\Psi_1=0.−KΨ1​−λCΨ1​=λ2MΨ1​⟹(λ2M+λC+K)Ψ1​=0.

Thus, Ψ1\Psi_1Ψ1​ is a null vector of Z(λ)Z(\lambda)Z(λ). It is a mode shape ϕm\phi_mϕm​, and the state eigenvector is

Ψm=[ϕmλmϕm],Z(λm)ϕm=0.\Psi_m=\begin{bmatrix}\phi_m\\\lambda_m\phi_m\end{bmatrix},\qquad Z(\lambda_m)\phi_m=0.Ψm​=[ϕm​λm​ϕm​​],Z(λm​)ϕm​=0.

Each nonzero solution of the quadratic problem also gives a state eigenvector. This vector has ϕm\phi_mϕm​ above λmϕm\lambda_m\phi_mλm​ϕm​. The correspondence is exact:

Z(λm)ϕm=0⟺A[ϕmλmϕm]=λm[ϕmλmϕm].Z(\lambda_m)\phi_m=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad A\begin{bmatrix}\phi_m\\\lambda_m\phi_m\end{bmatrix}=\lambda_m\begin{bmatrix}\phi_m\\\lambda_m\phi_m\end{bmatrix}.Z(λm​)ϕm​=0⟺A[ϕm​λm​ϕm​​]=λm​[ϕm​λm​ϕm​​].

In the quadratic problem, λm\lambda_mλm​ selects the matrix Z(λm)Z(\lambda_m)Z(λm​). The vector ϕm\phi_mϕm​ is in its nullspace. It does not satisfy Z(λm)ϕm=λmϕmZ(\lambda_m)\phi_m=\lambda_m\phi_mZ(λm​)ϕm​=λm​ϕm​. The first nnn entries of the state eigenvector give the displacement mode shape.

The two problems have the same 2n2n2n eigenvalues, with repeated roots counted by multiplicity. Real matrices give conjugate pairs of nonreal roots. A defective eigenvalue has fewer independent eigenvectors than its multiplicity. Its time response also requires polynomial factors. The simple-pole expansion on this page excludes that case.

The state form also shows why the exponential ansatz is sufficient. The solution of z˙=Az\dot z=Azz˙=Az is a matrix exponential. It is a combination of eλte^{\lambda t}eλt terms, with polynomial factors for defective eigenvalues.

A.1Damped modal parameters and undamped structural frequencies

The phrase “remove the damping” has two meanings. For the equivalent scalar oscillator, we set its damping ratio to zero. We keep the frequency parameter ωn,m=∣λm∣\omega_{n,m}=|\lambda_m|ωn,m​=∣λm​∣. For the whole structure, we set C=0C=0C=0 in (2.7) and solve a new eigenproblem. Let Ωr\Omega_rΩr​ be an undamped angular frequency and ψr\psi_rψr​ its displacement shape. Substitution of q=ψejΩtq=\psi e^{j\Omega t}q=ψejΩt into the undamped equation gives

Mq¨+Kq=0,Kψr=Ωr2Mψr.M\ddot q+Kq=0,\qquad K\psi_r=\Omega_r^2M\psi_r.Mq¨​+Kq=0,Kψr​=Ωr2​Mψr​.
(A.3)

This is a generalized symmetric eigenproblem. The matrix M−1KM^{-1}KM−1K is not symmetric in the ordinary inner product. It is symmetric in the MMM-inner product. Its eigenvalues are real and nonnegative when M≻0M\succ0M≻0 and K⪰0K\succeq0K⪰0. For one mass and spring, (A.3) and the scalar oscillator both give k/μ\sqrt{k/\mu}k/μ​.

The two frequencies also agree mode by mode for proportional damping, C=aM+bKC=aM+bKC=aM+bK, where a,ba,ba,b are constants. Apply Z(λ)Z(\lambda)Z(λ) to an undamped mode ψr\psi_rψr​. Then use Kψr=Ωr2MψrK\psi_r=\Omega_r^2M\psi_rKψr​=Ωr2​Mψr​:

Z(λ)ψr=(λ2M+λaM+λbK+K)ψr=[λ2+aλ+Ωr2(1+bλ)]Mψr.Z(\lambda)\psi_r=\left(\lambda^2M+\lambda aM+\lambda bK+K\right)\psi_r=\left[\lambda^2+a\lambda+\Omega_r^2(1+b\lambda)\right]M\psi_r.Z(λ)ψr​=(λ2M+λaM+λbK+K)ψr​=[λ2+aλ+Ωr2​(1+bλ)]Mψr​.
(A.4)

Since Mψr≠0M\psi_r\ne0Mψr​=0, the bracket must vanish. It is a quadratic in λ\lambdaλ,

λ2+(a+bΩr2)λ+Ωr2=0.\lambda^2+(a+b\Omega_r^2)\lambda+\Omega_r^2=0.λ2+(a+bΩr2​)λ+Ωr2​=0.

Comparison with λ2+2ζrΩrλ+Ωr2\lambda^2+2\zeta_r\Omega_r\lambda+\Omega_r^2λ2+2ζr​Ωr​λ+Ωr2​ gives ωn,r=Ωr\omega_{n,r}=\Omega_rωn,r​=Ωr​ and ζr=(a/Ωr+bΩr)/2\zeta_r=(a/\Omega_r+b\Omega_r)/2ζr​=(a/Ωr​+bΩr​)/2. The damped mode has the undamped shape with an added decay. The two definitions of natural frequency agree.

For general damping, the damped modes can combine several undamped shapes. Also, ∣λm∣|\lambda_m|∣λm​∣ is not necessarily equal to an Ωr\Omega_rΩr​. On this page, “natural frequency of mode mmm” means the equivalent-oscillator parameter ωn,m=∣λm∣\omega_{n,m}=|\lambda_m|ωn,m​=∣λm​∣.

BThe residue formula via the adjugate

Section 4.4 shows that the residue is rank one. It gives the input-coupling vector γm\gamma_mγm​ as a limit. This appendix evaluates that limit. The result gives a formula for implementations. It also shows when a mode is absent from the transfer matrix.

A cofactor belongs to row iii and column jjj of a square matrix. Remove that row and column, then calculate the determinant of the remaining matrix. The cofactor is (−1)i+j(-1)^{i+j}(−1)i+j times that determinant. The adjugate adj⁡Z\operatorname{adj}ZadjZ is the transpose of the cofactor matrix. It is also defined for singular matrices and satisfies

Zadj⁡Z=adj⁡Z Z=(det⁡Z)I.Z\operatorname{adj}Z=\operatorname{adj}Z\,Z=(\det Z)I.ZadjZ=adjZZ=(detZ)I.
(B.1)

Wherever ZZZ is invertible, Z−1=adj⁡Z/det⁡ZZ^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}Z/\det ZZ−1=adjZ/detZ. The transfer matrix is therefore

H(s)=Ladj⁡Z(s)det⁡Z(s)B.H(s)=L\frac{\operatorname{adj}Z(s)}{\det Z(s)}B.H(s)=LdetZ(s)adjZ(s)​B.

At a simple root λm\lambda_mλm​, the determinant has a simple zero. The adjugate has rank one. To see this, use (B.1). At the root, det⁡Z=0\det Z=0detZ=0, so Zadj⁡Z=0Z\operatorname{adj}Z=0ZadjZ=0. Each column of the adjugate is in the one-dimensional nullspace of Z(λm)Z(\lambda_m)Z(λm​). The adjugate is not zero because the root is simple. Thus,

adj⁡Z(λm)=cm ϕmℓmH,\operatorname{adj}Z(\lambda_m)=c_m\,\phi_m\ell_m^H,adjZ(λm​)=cm​ϕm​ℓmH​,
(B.2)

where cm≠0c_m\ne0cm​=0 is a constant. The right null vector ϕm\phi_mϕm​ satisfies Z(λm)ϕm=0Z(\lambda_m)\phi_m=0Z(λm​)ϕm​=0. The left null vector ℓmH\ell_m^HℓmH​ satisfies ℓmHZ(λm)=0\ell_m^HZ(\lambda_m)=0ℓmH​Z(λm​)=0. Both null vectors are nonzero because the root is simple.

Near the root, expand the determinant in a Taylor series. Let dm′d'_mdm′​ be its derivative at λm\lambda_mλm​. Then

det⁡Z(s)=(s−λm)dm′+O ⁣((s−λm)2).\det Z(s)=(s-\lambda_m)d'_m+O\!\left((s-\lambda_m)^2\right).detZ(s)=(s−λm​)dm′​+O((s−λm​)2).
(B.3)

Near the root, the remainder O((s−λm)2)O((s-\lambda_m)^2)O((s−λm​)2) is bounded by a constant times ∣s−λm∣2|s-\lambda_m|^2∣s−λm​∣2. Jacobi’s identity gives the derivative. The identity is also valid for singular matrices:

dm′=tr⁡ ⁣(adj⁡Z(λm)Z′(λm)),Z′(s)=2sM+C.d'_m=\operatorname{tr}\!\left(\operatorname{adj}Z(\lambda_m)Z'(\lambda_m)\right),\qquad Z'(s)=2sM+C.dm′​=tr(adjZ(λm​)Z′(λm​)),Z′(s)=2sM+C.

Substitution of (B.2) into the trace gives dm′=cmℓmH(2λmM+C)ϕmd'_m=c_m\ell_m^H(2\lambda_mM+C)\phi_mdm′​=cm​ℓmH​(2λm​M+C)ϕm​. In the residue limit, the factors s−λms-\lambda_ms−λm​ cancel. The constants cmc_mcm​ also cancel:

Rm=lim⁡s→λm(s−λm)H(s)=Ladj⁡Z(λm)Bdm′=(Lϕm)(ℓmHB)ℓmH(2λmM+C)ϕm=vmγmT.R_m=\lim_{s\to\lambda_m}(s-\lambda_m)H(s)=\frac{L\operatorname{adj}Z(\lambda_m)B}{d'_m}=\frac{(L\phi_m)(\ell_m^HB)}{\ell_m^H(2\lambda_mM+C)\phi_m}=v_m\gamma_m^T.Rm​=s→λm​lim​(s−λm​)H(s)=dm′​LadjZ(λm​)B​=ℓmH​(2λm​M+C)ϕm​(Lϕm​)(ℓmH​B)​=vm​γmT​.
(B.4)

Thus the input-coupling vector is

γmT=ℓmHBℓmH(2λmM+C)ϕm.\gamma_m^T=\frac{\ell_m^HB}{\ell_m^H(2\lambda_mM+C)\phi_m}.γmT​=ℓmH​(2λm​M+C)ϕm​ℓmH​B​.

The denominator is nonzero at a simple root. If it were zero, the determinant derivative would be zero and the root would not be simple. The residue is zero if Lϕm=0L\phi_m=0Lϕm​=0, so the mode is unobserved. It is also zero if ℓmHB=0\ell_m^HB=0ℓmH​B=0, so the mode is unexcited.

In a minimal state realization, each state direction is reachable from the inputs and observable in the outputs. Thus, the transfer matrix retains every state pole. Individual entries can still omit modes.

Let Hy˙H_{\dot y}Hy˙​​ and Hy¨H_{\ddot y}Hy¨​​ be the force-to-velocity and force-to-acceleration transfer matrices. With zero initial conditions, a time derivative gives a factor of sss. Thus, Hy˙=sHH_{\dot y}=sHHy˙​​=sH and Hy¨=s2HH_{\ddot y}=s^2HHy¨​​=s2H. The high-frequency limit of Hy¨H_{\ddot y}Hy¨​​ is the feedthrough LM−1BLM^{-1}BLM−1B. Equivalently, Hy¨=LM−1B+H~(s)H_{\ddot y}=LM^{-1}B+\tilde H(s)Hy¨​​=LM−1B+H~(s), where H~(s)→0\tilde H(s)\to0H~(s)→0 as s→∞s\to\inftys→∞.

The velocity and acceleration residues have factors λm\lambda_mλm​ and λm2\lambda_m^2λm2​, respectively. The feedthrough adds a constant term with no pole. Real or repeated roots require a different expansion. If the modal sum includes only a few modes, it has a residual.

Inverse expansion: [1], §3.5, equation (3.11). Factorized residues: [3], equations (2)–(3). The adjugate calculation supplies the intermediate steps.

CA bound on the omitted response

This appendix repeats the bound in §6.3 with the same notation. Assume that the force spectral matrix GxG_xGx​ is constant across the band. Let QxQ_xQx​ denote this matrix. Let Qx1/2Q_x^{1/2}Qx1/2​ be its Hermitian positive-semidefinite square root. Define the selected term and remainder, weighted by the excitation:

P=vmγmTjω−λm,E=Em(jω),Pw=PQx1/2,Ew=EQx1/2.P=\frac{v_m\gamma_m^T}{j\omega-\lambda_m},\qquad E=E_m(j\omega),\qquad P_w=PQ_x^{1/2},\qquad E_w=EQ_x^{1/2}.P=jω−λm​vm​γmT​​,E=Em​(jω),Pw​=PQx1/2​,Ew​=EQx1/2​.
(C.1)

Expansion of (5.3) gives

Gy=PwPwH+PwEwH+EwPwH+EwEwH.G_y=P_wP_w^H+P_wE_w^H+E_wP_w^H+E_wE_w^H.Gy​=Pw​PwH​+Pw​EwH​+Ew​PwH​+Ew​EwH​.

Let ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_2∥⋅∥2​ be the matrix spectral norm. The triangle inequality and the submultiplicative property ∥AB∥2≤∥A∥2∥B∥2\|AB\|_2\le\|A\|_2\|B\|_2∥AB∥2​≤∥A∥2​∥B∥2​ give

∥Gy−PwPwH∥2≤2∥Pw∥2∥Ew∥2+∥Ew∥22.\left\|G_y-P_wP_w^H\right\|_2\le2\|P_w\|_2\|E_w\|_2+\|E_w\|_2^2.​Gy​−Pw​PwH​​2​≤2∥Pw​∥2​∥Ew​∥2​+∥Ew​∥22​.

If ∥Ew∥2≤ε∥Pw∥2\|E_w\|_2\le\varepsilon\|P_w\|_2∥Ew​∥2​≤ε∥Pw​∥2​, then

∥Gy−PwPwH∥2≤(2ε+ε2)∥Pw∥22,∥Pw∥22=∥PwPwH∥2.\left\|G_y-P_wP_w^H\right\|_2\le(2\varepsilon+\varepsilon^2)\|P_w\|_2^2,\qquad \|P_w\|_2^2=\left\|P_wP_w^H\right\|_2.​Gy​−Pw​PwH​​2​≤(2ε+ε2)∥Pw​∥22​,∥Pw​∥22​=​Pw​PwH​​2​.
(C.2)

The second equality relates the bound to the size of the selected term. The condition on ε\varepsilonε is sufficient for an accurate rank-one approximation. It is not necessary. A matrix can be close to rank one even if this bound is loose.

The bound depends on the excitation. For a small ε\varepsilonε, the weighted omitted response must be small relative to the weighted selected response. Light damping alone does not ensure this condition.

DSpectral conventions and estimation

The main text uses one cross-spectrum convention and one spectral-density normalization. This appendix states both. It derives the normalization and describes effects on shape and damping estimates.

D.1Conjugation order

Some sources define the cross-spectral matrix with YˉYT\bar YY^TYˉYT instead of YYHYY^HYYH. Let G~y\widetilde G_yGy​ denote that matrix. Since YH=YˉTY^H=\bar Y^TYH=YˉT,

G~y=YˉYT=GyT=Gˉy.\widetilde G_y=\bar YY^T=G_y^T=\bar G_y.Gy​=YˉYT=GyT​=Gˉy​.
(D.1)

With this convention, the rank-one term is G~y≈dmvˉmvmT\widetilde G_y\approx d_m\bar v_mv_m^TGy​≈dm​vˉm​vmT​. The leading vector estimates vˉm\bar v_mvˉm​. Its conjugate gives the shape convention on this page. Both conventions are valid, but one calculation must use the same convention throughout.

SciPy’s csd(a, b) uses conjugate-first order. If y[i] contains channel iii, csd(y[j], y[i]) gives entry (i,j)(i,j)(i,j) of this page’s matrix. [6]

D.2Welch’s estimate

Welch’s method divides a record into segments. The segments can overlap. The method applies the same window to each channel and averages the spectral products. Detrending removes a fitted mean or trend. A window gives each sample a real weight. This controls spectral spreading from a finite record.

Let NbN_bNb​ be the number of segments and NwN_wNw​ their length in samples. Let w[ν]w[\nu]w[ν] be the window at index ν\nuν within a segment. The indices bbb and kkk identify segments and frequency bins. Let Yb[k]Y_b[k]Yb​[k] be the vector of unnormalized discrete Fourier transform (DFT) coefficients after detrending and windowing. A fast Fourier transform (FFT) computes the DFT.

The one-sided factor ηk\eta_kηk​ is 222 at interior positive-frequency bins. It is 111 at DC and at Nyquist, when present. At sampling rate fsf_sfs​, the estimate is

G^y+[k]=ηkNbfs∑ν=0Nw−1w[ν]2∑b=1NbYb[k]Yb[k]H.\widehat G_y^+[k]=\frac{\eta_k}{N_b f_s\sum_{\nu=0}^{N_w-1}w[\nu]^2}\sum_{b=1}^{N_b}Y_b[k]Y_b[k]^H.Gy+​[k]=Nb​fs​∑ν=0Nw​−1​w[ν]2ηk​​b=1∑Nb​​Yb​[k]Yb​[k]H.
(D.2)

A white-noise example shows the normalization. Assume a white channel with variance σ2\sigma^2σ2 and sampling rate fsf_sfs​. Its two-sided PSD is constant: G=σ2/fsG=\sigma^2/f_sG=σ2/fs​. The integral over the Nyquist band [−fs/2,fs/2][-f_s/2,f_s/2][−fs​/2,fs​/2] is Gfs=σ2Gf_s=\sigma^2Gfs​=σ2. For one segment, the expected squared magnitude of the windowed DFT coefficient is E∣Yb[k]∣2=σ2∑νw[ν]2\mathbb E|Y_b[k]|^2=\sigma^2\sum_\nu w[\nu]^2E∣Yb​[k]∣2=σ2∑ν​w[ν]2. Substitute G=σ2/fsG=\sigma^2/f_sG=σ2/fs​:

E∣Yb[k]∣2=G fs∑ν=0Nw−1w[ν]2.\mathbb E|Y_b[k]|^2=G\,f_s\sum_{\nu=0}^{N_w-1}w[\nu]^2.E∣Yb​[k]∣2=Gfs​ν=0∑Nw​−1​w[ν]2.

Division by fs∑w2f_s\sum w^2fs​∑w2 therefore gives an unbiased estimate of GGG. The average over NbN_bNb​ segments reduces its variance. The factor ηk\eta_kηk​ converts the two-sided density to the one-sided convention. For a colored signal, the window convolves the spectrum. Thus, the estimate is a smoothed version of the true density. The normalization preserves the integral, but not the exact shape.

Identical segments and windows preserve the Hermitian positive-semidefinite structure. Each segment contributes at most one independent direction to the average. Thus, the estimated rank cannot exceed NbN_bNb​. This limit comes from finite data and is not a physical rank.

The average reduces variability between estimates. It does not remove a persistent noise or forcing spectrum. Longer segments improve frequency resolution. More effectively independent segments improve the average. Overlap does not make segments independent.

Zeros added before the DFT give more samples of the same windowed spectrum. They do not improve the resolution set by the segment duration and window. [5]

D.3Density units and the inverse transform

The spectra on this page are densities per hertz. The superscripts (f)(f)(f) and (ω)(\omega)(ω) identify densities per hertz and per radian per second. The change of variables dω=2π dfd\omega=2\pi\,dfdω=2πdf gives

G(ω)(ω)=12πG(f) ⁣(ω2π).G^{(\omega)}(\omega)=\frac{1}{2\pi}G^{(f)}\!\left(\frac{\omega}{2\pi}\right).G(ω)(ω)=2π1​G(f)(2πω​).
(D.3)

For the EFDD inverse transform, mirror the one-sided spectrum to negative frequencies before the inverse DFT. Halve the one-sided interior positive bins. Copy them to the corresponding negative bins. Keep the DC and Nyquist endpoint weights from (D.2).

The inverse DFT has a normalization of 1/N1/N1/N. The frequency spacing is Δf=fs/N\Delta f=f_s/NΔf=fs​/N. The inverse transform sums Δf G[k]ej2πkℓ/N\Delta f\,G[k]e^{j2\pi k\ell/N}ΔfG[k]ej2πkℓ/N. Thus, the correlation is fsf_sfs​ times the inverse DFT of the mirrored spectrum.

Normalization by Rm(0)\mathcal R_m(0)Rm​(0) removes an overall scale. It does not correct incorrect mirroring or endpoint weights. Incorrect one-sided scaling can bias the damping estimate. [5]

D.4Additive sensor noise

Let η(t)\eta(t)η(t) denote sensor noise and GηG_\etaGη​ its PSD. If the noise and structural response have zero cross-covariance at every lag, their spectra add:

Gy+η=Gy+Gη.G_{y+\eta}=G_y+G_\eta.Gy+η​=Gy​+Gη​.
(D.4)

Correlated noise adds cross terms. Thus, a large singular value can also come from the measurement process. Noise raises all singular values. It has a proportionally larger effect on the smaller values. Thus, it reduces the ratio s1/s2s_1/s_2s1​/s2​ used for the rank-one interpretation.

EA perturbation bound for the leading singular vector

Section 7.2 states that a small perturbation gives a leading singular vector close to the physical shape. This appendix gives a bound for that statement. The Davis–Kahan theorem gives a sharper form that uses the spectral gap. [11]

Let G=G0+EG=G_0+EG=G0​+E be Hermitian. Let G0=d vvHG_0=d\,vv^HG0​=dvvH, ∥v∥=1\|v\|=1∥v∥=1, and d>0d>0d>0. Let uuu be a unit eigenvector of GGG for its largest eigenvalue λ1\lambda_1λ1​. Assume that λ1>0\lambda_1>0λ1​>0. Divide uuu into a component along vvv and a component orthogonal to vvv:

u=αv+βw,w⊥v,∥w∥=1,∣α∣2+∣β∣2=1.u=\alpha v+\beta w,\qquad w\perp v,\qquad \|w\|=1,\qquad |\alpha|^2+|\beta|^2=1.u=αv+βw,w⊥v,∥w∥=1,∣α∣2+∣β∣2=1.

The angle θ\thetaθ between uuu and vvv satisfies sin⁡θ=∣β∣\sin\theta=|\beta|sinθ=∣β∣. Because uuu is an eigenvector, Gu=λ1uGu=\lambda_1uGu=λ1​u. Take the inner product with www:

λ1β=wHGu=wH(G0+E)u.\lambda_1\beta=w^HGu=w^H(G_0+E)u.λ1​β=wHGu=wH(G0​+E)u.

Because w⊥vw\perp vw⊥v, the unperturbed term is zero: wHG0u=d wHv(vHu)=0w^HG_0u=d\,w^Hv(v^Hu)=0wHG0​u=dwHv(vHu)=0. Thus, λ1β=wHEu\lambda_1\beta=w^HEuλ1​β=wHEu. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives

∣β∣≤∥E∥2λ1,sin⁡θ≤∥E∥2λ1.|\beta|\le\frac{\|E\|_2}{\lambda_1},\qquad \sin\theta\le\frac{\|E\|_2}{\lambda_1}.∣β∣≤λ1​∥E∥2​​,sinθ≤λ1​∥E∥2​​.
(E.1)

This bound relates the angular error to the perturbation relative to the leading eigenvalue. When λ1\lambda_1λ1​ is approximately ddd, s1s_1s1​ estimates λ1\lambda_1λ1​. A large s1s_1s1​ relative to the perturbation is favorable.

A sharper form replaces λ1\lambda_1λ1​ by the gap between the first and second eigenvalues. If the leading eigenvalue is simple and the perturbation does not close the gap, the Davis–Kahan theorem gives

sin⁡θ≤∥E∥2λ1−λ2.\sin\theta\le\frac{\|E\|_2}{\lambda_1-\lambda_2}.sinθ≤λ1​−λ2​∥E∥2​​.

When the second eigenvalue is close to the first, the denominator is small and the bound is weak. Thus, a ratio s1/s2s_1/s_2s1​/s2​ near one leaves the direction undetermined. A large gap can make the direction stable even if the absolute perturbation is not very small. The bound is sufficient, not necessary. A direction can be stable for reasons that this inequality does not capture.

FSources for the derivations

The table identifies sources for the results and algebra in this page. The equations on this page give the numerical examples and interactive figures. Equation numbers use section numbers. Thus, an added derivation in one section does not change the numbers in other sections.

DerivationSource
Energy and equation of motion (2.1)–(2.9)Derived here from the stated quadratic energy forms and Lagrange’s equations. The matrix symmetry and definiteness arguments are worked out in §2.4.
Quadratic eigenproblem (3.1)–(3.2), state form (A.1)–(A.4)[1], introduction and §§3.4–3.6. Substitution, block calculation, and the proportional-damping reduction shown here.
Pole parameters (3.7), free response (3.8)[9], §2, for the scalar oscillator; [3], §2, for modal parameters. Coefficient matching and initial-condition solutions shown here.
Laplace transform (4.1)–(4.2), transfer matrix (4.4)[10] for the transform; [2] for transfer functions and minimal realizations. Integration by parts and the matrix inversion shown here.
Residues (4.5)–(4.9), adjugate proof (B.1)–(B.4)[1], §3.5; [3], equations (2)–(3). The adjugate calculation supplies the intermediate steps.
PSD (5.1)–(5.3), Welch estimate (D.2)[5] and [6]. Matrix positivity, normalization, and the one-sided scaling worked out here.
Rank-one approximation (6.1)–(6.4), residual bound (C.1)–(C.2)[3], §§2–3. The four-term expansion and the norm bound are derived here.
FDD (7.1)–(7.8), perturbation bound (E.1)[3], §3; [4], close-mode examples; [11] for the gap form. Eigenpair, peak location, and two-mode calculations derived here.
EFDD (8.1)–(8.3)[4], p. 699; [7]. Correlation scaling and decrement algebra shown here; leakage discussed in [8].
